chunks: Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Musa (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Muhammad ibn Abi Abdullah al-Kufi said: He narrated to me Al-Hussein ibn Ubaydullah al-Ash'ari said: He narrated to me Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from Al-Qasim ibn Yahya, from his grandfather Al-Hasan ibn Rashid, from Al-Mufaddal ibn Umar

He said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'How many festive days do the Muslims have?' He replied: 'Four.' I said: 'I know of the two Eids and Friday.' He said to me: 'The greatest and most noble of them is the eighteenth of Dhul-Hijja, which is the day on which the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) appointed the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) and established him as a sign for the people.' I said: 'What is incumbent upon us on that day?' He said: 'It is incumbent upon you to fast in gratitude and praise to God, even though He deserves to be thanked every hour. And thus the Prophets commanded their Trustees to fast on the day the Trustee is appointed, making it an Eid. Whoever fasts on that day, it is better than the deeds of sixty years.' The word of God, the Mighty and Majestic, to Ibrahim: 'So take four birds and commit them to yourself…'

key_terms.أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (title for Ali ibn Abi Talib)
key_terms.ذِي الْحِجَّةِ: Dhul-Hijja (the twelfth month of the Islamic lunar calendar)
key_terms.صِيَامُهُ: Fasting on it (referring to the specific day)

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the eighteenth of Dhul-Hijja and the ruling on fasting for it according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In al-Khisal, Shaykh al-Saduq records Imam al-Sadiq identifying Eid al-Ghadir (18th Dhul-Hijja) as the preeminent of four Islamic festivals, marking the public appointment of Ali ibn Abi Talib as the definitive proof (Hujjah) for the community. The narration emphasizes that fasting on this day is obligatory (Wajib) as an act of gratitude, equating its reward to sixty years of worship, and links this tradition to the precedent of Prophets appointing their successors. The concluding reference to Ibrahim’s four birds (2:260) is interpreted by Shia scholars as a symbolic allusion to these four festive occasions established through divine appointment.
